title: The lump of clay
hookLine: a young man comes home from his studies proud, and his father asks one question he can't answer
carry: one clay under every name and form

cards: A son walks back into his father's house after years away at study. He has learned the Vedas. He carries himself like someone who has finished.

The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't flatter him: it says he came home proud, thinking himself learned. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question, and the son, Shvetaketu, who knows so much, has no idea what his father means.
Year two walked through this scene. It comes back today, one day before the year closes, as the doorway to the last of the ranges ahead: the great sayings.

teach.h: THE TEACHING THAT MAKES THE UNHEARD HEARD.
teach.b: Here's the question, in paraphrase: did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu says, sir, what kind of teaching is that?
So his father gives him a picture.
By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot, the cup, the lamp: the difference is a name, a way of speaking. What's real is the clay.
Then comes the line that makes the scene. Shvetaketu says, in effect: surely my teachers didn't know this, or why wouldn't they have told me?
Teach me, sir. He came home finished. One question later, he's a beginner again.
What follows is a long teaching. In the beginning, the father says, there was only being, sat, one without a second.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.
teach.b: And again and again he ends with a short phrase: tat tvam asi, that you are. Tradition counts it among the great sayings. Here's the teaching, plainly.

teach.h: ONE CLAY, EVERY NAME AND FORM.
teach.b: Vedanta calls that one being Brahman: the clay under every name and form, under the many gods of yesterday, and under you. And it isn't gathered like facts.
It's asked for, humbly, from a teacher, which is why Hindus honor the guru, and why even a proud graduate starts again with: teach me, sir.

how: The dialogue between Uddalaka and Shvetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta as the setting of the saying tat tvam asi, and some Hindu teachers retell it as a lesson in a student's humility.

games.q: you're Shvetaketu, home from years of study. your father asks about a teaching you've never heard of. what do you do?
o: recite everything you learned to prove you're finished.
say your teachers can't have known it, and ask him to teach you.
change the subject and leave the room.
games.why: he says, in effect, surely my teachers didn't know this. teach me, sir. the proud graduate becomes a beginner, and the long teaching begins.

practice: Bring to mind one thing this path taught you this year, a story, a line, a practice, and hold it up like the lump of clay.
Don't recite it; ask what's underneath it that you haven't heard yet, then set it down and simply breathe, with nothing finished.
If you pray, you can bring the words teach me to God in your own way; if you don't, let the question stay with you through the sit.

wordCard.voice: Shvetaketu. The student who came home proud and thinking himself learned, and became a beginner again, asking to be taught the clay under everything.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tat tvam asi, 'that you are,' the saying Uddalaka repeats to Shvetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad.

carryVoice: Your line: one clay under every name and form. The proud graduate became a beginner, and that was the start. Year three is nearly done.
